I will now make a statement as the President of the General Assembly. Your Excellency, Lok Bawdui Thapa, President of ECOSOC, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. Eighty years ago, the United Nations was forged from the wreckage of war. to prevent future conflict and to confront the legacies of the past. And a few legacies were as bitter or as pervasive as colonialism. When we enshrined the principles of self-determination in the UN Charter, we made a radical break from history. We declared that the era of ruling people without their consent was over. In doing so, we lit a path to freedom for more than 750 million people. a third of the world's population back then, who in 1945 were still living under the shadow of foreign rule, including across more than 50 African countries that would go on to achieve independence in the decades that followed. Think of what this meant on the ground in societies where generation after generation had never known what it meant to be governed by their own people. For young persons coming of age in New Delhi, in Accra, or Jakarta, this promise marked a profound turning point. They could look forward to something their parents or grandparents may have had only dreamt of, a future shaped by their own choices, not by a distant capital. For a young person in Kingston, Port of Spain, or Suva, independence stopped being an abstract dream and became a horizon within reach. That expectation, shared across oceans, marked a global turning point. To turn that hope into reality, in 1960, this Assembly adopted the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and People. This text did more than affirm the rights of nations large and small. It spoke of dignity. It spoke of social progress. And it placed decolonization firmly where it belongs, as a shared responsibility of the whole international community. I was reminded myself of the weight of that responsibility last year while reflecting on what marked 140 years since the Berlin Conference of 1884, when European powers, including my own country, violently divided an entire continent without the presence or consent of its people. As I said at that time, we cannot undo what happened in the past. But we can work together to build a better future. To do so, it is crucial to identify and acknowledge injustice. For that injustice did not end with the closing of that conference over 100 years ago. It shaped borders, divided whole communities, fueled conflicts, and entrenched inequalities whose consequences remain with us today. And therefore, we have a common responsibility to address these consequences together. Today's meeting, following General Assembly resolution 80/106, which proclaimed 14 December as the International Day Against Colonialism in all its forms and manifestations, honors the declaration we committed to 65 years ago. By doing so, the General Assembly is underlining our shared responsibility to carry forward the work the Declaration sets in motion. That responsibility is especially urgent in the light of the fact that some global challenges, like climate change, economic fragility, and limited access to finance, place additional strain on some of the former colonialized societies. These issues remain also relevant for those non-self-governing territories who remain on the agenda of the Special Committee on Decolonization. As said, we cannot undo what we did in the past, but we can work together to build a better future. The eradication of colonialism in all its forms 55 years ago was this promise. by the Common Declaration, realizing that the promise remains our enduring responsibility. I have the honor to deliver the statement on behalf of the chair of the Special Committee on the Situation with Regards to the Implementation of the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples. As we gather to commemorate the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples, adopted 65 years ago, we affirm its historic and continued significance. This declaration is not merely a document of the past. It is a living commitment to decolonization. It reminds us that the continued existence of colonialism is incompatible with the Charter of the United Nations and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Its principles are as relevant today as they were in 1960. The declaration remains a guiding light to our collective efforts to eradicate colonialism, which continues to be one of the priorities of the United Nations. Over the decades, the Special Committee on Decolonization has played a leading role in advancing this agenda. Pursuant to our mandate, the C-24 actively advances the decolonization agenda through monitoring conditions in non-self-governing territories, organizing regional seminars, dispatching visiting missions, as well as providing the space for dialogue for relevant stakeholders, thereby ensuring that decolonization remains firmly on the UN's agenda. Yet, more than 16 years after the adoption of the declaration, its provisions have not been fully implemented. As we approach the end of the Fourth International Decade for the Eradication of Colonialism, we must acknowledge that progress has been too slow. And this reality compels us to create new momentum, revitalizing the role of the Committee. The General Assembly's recent adoption of resolution 80/106 is a milestone in this regard. The resolution proclaims 14 December as the International Day Against Colonialism in all its forms and manifestations, to be observed annually beginning in 2025. This solemn decision underscores the urgency of bringing colonialism to a speedy and unconditional end. To succeed, we need the active engagement of all actors, administering powers, the territories themselves, the UN system, and all member states. Constructive dialogue and cooperation are indispensable. In this regard, annual regional seminars and visiting missions remain vital tools for fostering understanding, building trust, and identifying practical solutions. Equally important is the provision of well-targeted support and assistance to non-self-governing territories, addressing their specific socioeconomic and environmental challenges. This support should be linked to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Pact for the Future, ensuring that our efforts to end colonialism also advance global development goals. Madam President, the Special Committee must work with renewed determination and creativity if it is to deliver concrete and meaningful results. The time for declarations alone have passed. What is needed now is cooperation and action. In this spirit and in line with resolution 80/106, I call upon all Member States, the UN system, regional organizations and civil society to actively observe the International Day Against Colonialism on 14 December each year and to use this occasion to reaffirm our shared commitment to the complete eradication of colonialism. Let us seize this opportunity marked by the first observance of the International Day, to bring the era of colonialism closer to its end. Thank you.

Parts of the world.

We align ourselves with the statement delivered by Uganda on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. Mr. President, Resolution 1514 stands as one of the most consequential acts of this Assembly, providing legal and moral weight to the decolonization process, impacting millions of lives and reshaping the international order. Its deeper significance lies in how it fundamentally transformed the role of the General Assembly itself, affirming that peace and security are inseparable from justice and that this chamber must remain a space where people, peoples long silenced, may find voice, dignity and redress. The adoption in 2020 of resolution 75/123 declaring 2021 to 2030 the fourth International Decade for the Eradication of Colonialism serves as a stark reminder that colonialism is not merely a historical injustice to be studied. It is a present and persistent reality demanding our urgent attention. It is in this connection that Mozambique is deeply concerned that 17 territories remain listed as non-self-governing, their people still awaiting the fulfilment of promises made decades ago. We are equally troubled that the peoples of Palestine and Western Sahara continue to be denied their inalienable right to self-determination. We also welcome the recent adoption of the resolution 18/106, establishing 14 December as the International Day Against Colonialism. This is an important milestone in the UN's longstanding commitment to bring colonialism in all its forms and manifestation to an unconditional end. Mr. President, the African Union's 2025 theme, justice for Africans and people of African descent through reparations, underscores the global imperative that the need to confront and address enduring wounds of colonialism, slavery, apartheid, and genocide. Mozambique's own history reminds us that colonial legacy casts long shadows, the inequalities and divisions that persist are not mere accidents of history, but inheritance of systems designed to exploit and subjugate. However, we also reject the prevailing narrative of post-independence Africa that remains too often steeped in pessimism, ranging from activism, to self-negation and self-flatteration, ignoring the complexity of our realities and the urgency of our people. The post-colonial project of genuine sovereignty does not end with the raising of a flag or casting of a vote. It is a daily, complex, and cumulative endeavor involving the building of institutions, managing diversity, educating the youth, and shaping rules around capital and technology that serve the common good. Mr. President, that is why Mozambique supports meaningful discussion on compensation and reparatory justice, not as a call for pity or charity, but as essential components of the broader global architecture of peace, fairness, and genuine reckoning with the past. I thank you, Mr. President.
Muito obrigado, distinguished representative of Mozambique. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ethiopia.

Mr. President, my delegation aligns itself with the statement delivered by Uganda on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. 65 years ago, the United Nations General Assembly, in its resolution 1514, adopted the historic declaration on the granting of independence to colonial countries and peoples. The declaration recognizes the fundamental human rights of all people, the right to self-determination, the inalienable rights of people's freedom, the exercise of their sovereignty, and the integrity of their national territory. The declaration also gives recognition to the social, cultural, economic impacts of colonialism and its impediments to development. The declaration gave momentum to great wave of independence that transformed Africa in the 1960s and the 1970s. Newly sovereign states joined this assembly, bringing with them the collective vision of a free and united Africa. The Pan-African spirit was not only about political independence. It was about solidarity, dignity, and the determination to build a continent free from exploitation and external domination. Ethiopia, as part of the Pan-African family of nations, played a pivotal role in this process. Ethiopia, as one of the few African nations never colonized, became a symbol of resilience and independence. And in 1960, It proudly co-sponsored resolution 1514. The adoption of this Declaration had obviously helped dismantle formal colonial systems. However, the fact that there are so many territories still listed as non-self-governing indicates to the unfinished business of decolonization. For these people, the promise of self-government is still deferred. We must therefore use today's anniversary to renew our collective commitment to ensure that these communities enjoy the freedom and pursue their economic, social, and cultural development without undue external interference. The commemoration of the declaration also coincides with the fourth International Decade for the Eradication of Colonialism, proclaimed for the year 2021-2030. It reminds us that the agenda of decolonization must get closure in the spirit of the principles of this declaration. In the meantime, lingering injustices originating from colonialism, such as non-representation of Africa in the permanent category of the UN Security Council, must be addressed without delay. Mr. President, the International Decade urges the need to accelerate progress, strengthen the role of the United Nations, in supporting self-determination and ensure that no territory or people are left behind in the march towards achieving the development objectives. As has been rightly stated by the Secretary General in his April 2025 report on the Fourth International Decade for the Eradication of Colonialism, fostering on a case-by-case basis transparent and constructive dialogue among non-self-governing territories, administering powers, Member States and other stakeholders is crucial. In conclusion, Ethiopia reiterates its commitment to the implementation of the International Decade and ensure that no people or region is left behind in achieving a dignified life free from all forms of colonialism, in all its forms and manifestations. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ethiopia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Pakistan.

Mr. President, we align with the statement delivered by Uganda on behalf of NAM. Pakistan joins Member States in commemorating the 65th anniversary of the adoption of General Assembly resolution 1514, the historic declaration on the granting of independence to colonial countries and peoples. The declaration unequivocally affirmed that the subjection of peoples to alien subjugation, domination, and exploitation constitutes a denial of fundamental human rights, is contrary to the Charter of the United Nations, and poses an impediment to the promotion of world peace and cooperation. It also established the right to self-determination as an inalienable and universal right. As the United Nations continues to serve as a beacon of hope and justice across the world, it must ensure the consistent and non-selective implementation of its resolutions, and uphold international law without exception. The implementation of the Declaration and the decolonization agenda is not confined to the non-self-governing territories alone. It also encompasses people living under alien occupation and foreign domination. The overarching objective, therefore, remains to ensure that all such peoples are enabled to exercise their inalienable right to self-determination. Mr. President, while the decolonization process stands among the United Nations' notable achievements, this anniversary also compels us to acknowledge that the promise of Resolution 1514 remains unfulfilled, posing a continuing challenge to the maintenance of international peace and security. The realization of self-determination is not merely a historical aspiration; it is an enduring obligation. Recent developments in the Middle East demonstrate that lasting peace cannot be achieved through the continued denial and suppression of the legitimate right to self-determination of the Palestinian people. Similarly, the UN Security Council has, through several resolutions, recognized the legitimate right of self-determination of the people of Jammu and Kashmir. A just resolution of the Jammu and Kashmir dispute remains central to the establishment of durable peace in South Asia. As we mark this solemn anniversary, Pakistan calls for renewed international resolve to fully and unconditionally eradicate colonialism in all its forms and manifestations. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Pakistan. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Israel.

Mr. President, for more than 800 days, Israel has said one thing clearly and consistently. The war in Gaza is not over until all the hostages are home, every last one. That is not a slogan. It is a promise. One name remains. Ran Gvili, murdered by Hamas terrorists on October 7th while defending innocent civilians. His body was abducted into Gaza, where it is still being held. Against all odds, Israel has brought 254 out of 255 hostages, we brought them back home. Some of you in this hall tried to move on from the hostages. You thought it's over. Israel refused to forget them. That is why 254 are home today, celebrating Hanukkah with their families. Let there be no doubt, we will not stop until we will bring Ran home. President Trump's plan said it very clearly. that all of them must come back home. Hamas chooses to blatantly violate the terms of the plan. Israel has acted in good faith. We have worked with the mediators. We have provided intelligence showing that Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad, they know exactly where Ran's body is being held. They can bring him back home immediately. On October 7th, Ran Gvili was 24 years old. When the massacre began, he left his home and bravely went out to confront the terrorists. As innocent people fled, he went toward danger. That choice defines who he is. On October 8th, Ran would have turned 25. Last week, I traveled to Israel. I met with Ron's family. I saw, I felt their pain. I also saw the strength and the resilience. They are still waiting for Ron to be returned to them so he can come home and be laid to rest with dignity. They do not stand alone. Our entire nation stands behind them, united in one demand: Bring Ron home. Today, with us, Ron's younger sister, Shira Gvili, is here with us at the United Nations. She has come with a message. Do not let the world accept a reality where even one hostage is left behind. A few nights ago, Shira stood at Ben Gurion Airport in Israel on her way to the UN. In our airport, until recently, you had a hall filled with the posters of the hostages. Today, only one poster remains, runs. When Shira returns home, let us pray she does not have to see that poster again. No, let us do more than pray. Let us put pressure where it belongs, on Hamas, on Palestinian Islamic Jihad, so that she never has to see that poster again. Shira, we tell you this today, we will not rest until your brother is returned home. Let me be very clear, we are committed to bringing Gran home no matter what, because when we make promises, We keep them. For more than 800 days, I have worn a hostage pin on my lapel. I have waited for the day I could remove it and stand here without it. That day has not yet come. As long as Ran Gvili has not been returned, it remains. Ran is not just a number. He is not a bargaining chip. is the test of whether this Chamber insists on basic humanity. Bring him home. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank you, the distinguished representative of Israel. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia.

Mr. President, I wish to start by quoting the first part of the preamble of Indonesia's national constitution. "Independence is the right of all nations, and therefore colonialism must be abolished in this world, as it is not in conformity with humanity and justice." This constitutional mandate is the one we always carry in our beliefs that colonialism has no place in our shared future. Therefore, it is in Indonesia's DNA to always be committed to the UN decolonization agenda. Our commitment has been reflected through the formulation of the 10 principles of Bandung, or Dasar Sila Bandung, adopted in 1955. Born in Bandung 60 years ago, those principles reflected the collective voice of newly independent nations in Asia and Africa that no people should live under subjugation, domination or exploitation. The spirit of Bandung helped shape a global political momentum that, five years later, culminated in the adoption of the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples. The Declaration marked a watershed moment in the history of the UN, and therefore, all Member States must demonstrate their unwavering political commitment and collective resolve for the implementation of the Declaration. Mr. President, today's commemoration of the Declaration must be more than a symbolic observance. It should be a renewed call to action. Millions of people in 70 non-self-governing territories continue to face marginalization, economic dependency, and constraints on their ability to determine their future. The full implementation of the Declaration thus remains a collective responsibility of the UN. This responsibility includes strengthening the role of the Special Committee on Decolonization, ensuring that the voices of the people concerned remain at the center of our efforts, and providing assistance and support aimed at achieving sustained and durable solutions in specific territories. At the same time, Indonesia wishes to underscore that the noble cause of decolonization must always be guided by the principles of the UN Charter that gives respect to sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national unity of member states. Mr. President, as we also observe the first International Day Against Colonialism this year, let us reaffirm our shared commitment to a world free from all forms of colonialism. Let us seize this momentum to strengthen our resolve to ensure that decolonization remains a force for peace, justice, and dignity for all people. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cambodia.

Cambodia aligns itself with the statement of the Non-Aligned Movement, and I wish to deliver this statement in my national capacity. The spirit of the International Days Against Colonialism in all its form and manifestations resonates profoundly with Cambodia's nation-building journey and coincides with our celebration of the 70th anniversary of our membership in the United Nations. For these past decades, Cambodia's position has remained consistent and principles. We strictly adhere to international law and United Nations charters, uphold the peaceful settlement of disputes, and respect territorial integrity and national sovereignties. These commitments are not only foundational to our national development, but also essential to the effective pursuit of peace and justice among all nations. We also recognize that the legacy of colonialism continues to shape societies and economies across the globe, underscoring the need for collective actions. Addressing these enduring impacts requires not only remembrance, but also a renewed commitment to dialogues, reconciliations, and cooperations. Cambodia, therefore, welcomes regional and international effort to build trust among nations, foster solidarities, and ensures that all countries can prosper together on an equal footing. This International Day is not only about reflecting on the past, but also about shaping our common futures. By commemorating it, we strongly We strengthened the foundation of multilateralism and reaffirmed our determination to confront and continue the impacts of colonialism. In doing so, we advanced the promise of equal rights, justice, and sustainable development for all peoples and territories subjected to colonial rules, as enshrined in the declaration adopted by this General Assembly 65 years ago. Mr. President, in closing, Cambodia affirms its readiness to work with Member States, the UN system, the relevant stakeholders to constructively contribute to UN initiatives and to support collective measures that build a world where Every nation can strive for peace, dignity, and full sovereignty. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cambodia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Timor-Leste.

Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President and Excellencies, as we commemorate the 65th anniversary of the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples, Timor-Leste approaches this high-level plenary meeting with deep respect and with gratitude for a declaration that reshaped history and restored dignity to millions, including us Timorese. Adopted in 1960, this landmark declaration ignited the global movement and affirm a simple yet profound truth. All peoples have the right to determine their own future. For Timor-Leste, a young nation shaped by colonial rule, prolonged occupation, and extraordinary international solidarity, this anniversary is not a distant milestone. It is a living principle. Our independence, restored in 2002 after decades of resistance, reflects the declaration core promise that the imposition of external will should not in any way deny the destiny of the people. The right to self-determination remains a cornerstone of international law enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and reaffirmed by this Assembly on numerous occasions. It is an inalienable and universal human right not a concession to be granted or withheld according to shifting geopolitical interests. 65 years on, we must acknowledge a troubling reality. In several non-self-governing territories, most notably the Western Sahara, this right continues to be delayed, diluted, or denied. People who seek to freely decide their political status and future face obstacles rooted in strategic calculations economic dependency, and misinformation. Such practices run counter to the spirit of the 1960 declaration and weaken our credibility when we speak of justice, equality, and the rule of law. Timor-Leste understands the struggle at human level. Our people paid a devastating price, life lost, families torn apart, communities displaced, and resources exploited for asserting rights that should never have been questioned. It was the United Nations' principled engagement through popular consultation and subsequent peacekeeping efforts that finally enabled our people to express their will and reclaim their sovereignty freely. That experience obliges us to speak with clarity today. The ambitions of powerful actors must never eclipse the legitimate aspirations of peoples in non-self-governing territories. Self-determination is not a negotiable privilege. It's a non-derogable right. When it is ignored or obstructed, instability deepens, injustice persists, and the foundation of the post-colonial international order are eroded. As we reflect on six and a half decades of progress, Timor Leste calls on the Assembly to renew its resolve. The international community must strengthen its support for the decolonization process and ensure that the Special Committee on Decolonization, C-24, is politically and institutionally equipped to fulfill its mandate effectively. Let us honor the 1960 Declaration not only in words, but through actions, by facilitating genuine and transparent self-determination processes, by protecting the voices of indigenous and local communities, by holding accountable those who seek to obstruct the processes through coercion, pressure, or disinformation. In doing so, we affirm the dignity of all peoples and move closer to a world free from the shadows of colonialism. Mr. President, Timor-Leste remains firmly committed to the principles of the United Nations and to the unfinished work of global decolonization. On this anniversary, we reaffirm our solidarity with all peoples who continue to seek independence and self-governments. We do so with confidence that together we can realize a future in which self-determination is not deferred, denied, or diminished, but fully realized everywhere. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Timor-Leste. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Trinidad and Tobago.

Thank you, Chair. Trinidad and Tobago aligns itself with the statement delivered on behalf of the CARICOM member states and the statement on behalf of the non-aligned movement. We are honored to join this commemoration of the 65th anniversary of the historic declaration on the granting of independence to colonial countries and peoples. This landmark resolution adopted by the General Assembly in 1960, affirmed the inalienable rights of all peoples to self-determination and independence, a principle that transformed the global order and gave hope to nations like ours, which achieved independence in 1962. The resolution signaled a turning point in the global struggle against colonialism and a cornerstone of the United Nations' commitment to equality, sovereignty, and human dignity. It gave voice to the aspirations of peoples long denied their rights and provided a framework for dismantling of colonial systems. Today, we pay tribute to those who fought tirelessly for freedom and to the United Nations for its unwavering support of decolonization. Yet, as we mark this anniversary, we must acknowledge that the work remains unfinished. There are still non-self-governing territories who await the full realization of their right of self-determination. The international community must renew its commitment to completing the decolonization agenda guided by the principles of dialogue, respect for the wishes of the peoples concerned, and adherence to international law. Trinidad and Tobago reaffirms its solidarity with all peoples striving for independence and calls for strengthened cooperation between member states, the Special Committee on Decolonization, and the administering powers to accelerate progress. We also underscore the importance of addressing the lingering legacies of colonialism, economic dependence, structural inequities, and cultural erasures, which continue to impede sustainable development. As we look ahead, let us recommit to the vision enshrined in the declaration, a world where all nations, large and small, exercise sovereignty, free from domination, and where the principles of equality and justice prevail. I thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Trinidad and Tobago. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Algeria.

Thank you, President. Algeria aligns itself with the declaration made by the Non-Aligned Movement. But we want to add on our national capacity the following. President, we meet today to commemorate the International Day for the eradication of colonialism in all its forms and manifestations. A day that compels not only remembrance, but reckoning. Colonialism was never merely a political or a military enterprise. It was a comprehensive system of domination, of oppression, designed to erase identities, to erase cultures, to dismantle civilizations, and to exhaust the capacities of colonized people. As Frantz Fanon so powerfully described it, colonialism is, I quote, "violence in its raw state." Africa has suffered the most of colonialism. In this sense, The International Conference on the Crimes of Colonialism in Africa, held in Algiers just recently, marked a major step in addressing historical justice, as reflected in the Algiers Declaration. Mr. President, when General Assembly Resolution 1514 was adopted, one must ask whether its architect could have imagined that more than six decades later, we would still be debating the persistence of colonialism. We will still confronting the reality that entire peoples remain denied their inalienable rights to self-determination, to freedom. Yet, here you are. 65 years later, some peoples continue to endure grave violations of their fundamental rights and human dignity, conditions that represent not only an affront to international law, but a profound regression in human history. Mr. President, today's commemoration is, first and foremost, an occasion to honor the struggle of people living under foreign occupation, to remember their suffering, and to reaffirm our unwavering solidarity with them in Palestine, in Western Sahara, and elsewhere in all remaining non-self-governing territories. But it must also be a moment of collective courage, a moment to honestly ask ourselves difficult, questions. Why has the decolonization process remained unfinished?

Thank you, Mr. President. At the outset, Japan would like to emphasize one of the purposes of the UN enshrined in Article 1 of the Charter, to develop friendly relations among nations based on respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples. In this spirit, in 1960, the General Assembly proclaimed in its resolution the necessity of bringing to a speedy and unconditional end colonialism in all forms and manifestations. Since then, friendly relations declaration and international covenants on human rights were adopted. Through these developments, the colonial people's right of self-determination to seek liberation from imperialist states governing them and attain independence or separate political status has been legally established. We shall abandon colonial rule forever and respect the right of self-determination of all peoples throughout the world. Japan will continue to make unceasing efforts towards the full realization of this right within the international community. Mr. President, it is regrettable that the Chinese delegation made a groundless statement against Japan. Since the end of World War II, Japan has consistently followed the path of peace-loving nation and made innumerable contribution to the peace and prosperity of international community. With respect to China's unsubstantiated claims regarding history, I will refrain from refuting each one individually. The current administration has upheld in its entirety the positions of previous Japanese cabinets on history and will continue to do so. On China's claim on Japan's defense posture, Japan's position is already stated in my letters dated November 24 and December 4, addressed to the Secretary General and also circulated to the member states in response to the two letters from the permanent representative of China. Japan's fundamental defense policy is the posture of passive defense strategy, which is exclusively defense oriented. China's assertion that Japan would exercise the right of self-defense even in the absence of armed attack is erroneous. I would like to reiterate Japan's fundamental stance regarding Taiwan, which is articulated in the Japan-China Joint Communique of 1972. we reiterate our consistent position of expecting that issues concerning Taiwan will be resolved peacefully through dialogue. To conclude, Japan believes the differences of views should be addressed through dialogue, for that is an core of the spirit of UN Charter. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Japan. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Argentina.

President, the Argentine Republic is pleased to participate at this high-level meeting to commemorate the 65th anniversary of the adoption of resolution 1514 by the General Assembly. This resolution stated the need to bring a swift and unconditional end to colonialism in all of its forms and manifestations. It made clear that there is more than one form of colonialism, and it established different principles such as self-determination and territorial integrity to address different cases. It also established that total or partial violation of the territorial integrity of a country contravenes the purposes and principles of the Charter. President, this very week, on Tuesday, December 16, there was also another anniversary, the 60th anniversary of resolution 2065, the first resolution adopted by this organization relating to the question of the Malvinas Islands. It applied the tenets of resolution 1514 to this specific and particular colonial situation. In 1965, the General Assembly determined that the decolonization of this territory should be tackled through negotiations between Argentina and the United Kingdom to resolve the sovereignty dispute over the islands, and that the principle of self-determination was not applicable to this case. Since then, the United Nations has renewed this call multiple times, and it remains in force today. We regret that, despite the amount of time that has passed and Argentina's total willingness to comply with this mandate, the United Kingdom persists in its attitude of ignoring the call to return to the negotiating table. The failure to resolve this dispute is compounded by the unjustified and disproportionate military presence and the illegal and unilateral exploitation of renewable and non-renewable natural resources in the area claimed by the United Kingdom. Such actions are in breach of resolutions 41/11 and 31/49 of this Assembly. Just a few days ago, on December 11, the Argentine Foreign Ministry issued a statement rejecting the final investment decision announced by the illegitimate licensees, Rockhopper Exploration PLC, a British entity, and Navitas Petroleum, an Israeli entity, to develop the Sea Lion field in the North Malvinas Basin without Argentina's authorization. The Argentine Republic reserves the right to apply all measures available to prevent this and to defend its sovereign rights and interests. President, I wish to reiterate my country's full readiness to resume negotiations and to seek a solution that will allow us to bring an end to this protracted sovereignty dispute over the Malvinas, South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands and the surrounding maritime areas. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Argentina. Distinguished delegates, we have four remaining speakers on the list. I hereby close the list of speakers. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of United Republic of Tanzania.

President, esteemed delegates, the United Republic of Tanzania is proud to join the global community to commemorate the 65th anniversary of the Declaration on the granting of independence to colonial countries and people. President, Tanzania's own history is a testament to the power of decolonization. We recall the tireless effort of our founding father who fought against colonial rule to birth a nation built on unity, equality, and justice. Today, we stand in solidarity with the peoples around the globe. and all non-self-governing territories who still yearn for the same freedoms we enjoy. On the occasion of the 65th anniversary of the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and People, we reflect on the progress made towards decolonization and challenges that remains. The declaration adopted by United Nations General Assembly in 1960 marked a significant milestone in the struggle for independence and self-determination of colonial territories. It recognized the right of the peoples to freedom, independence, and self-governance. Six decades later, much has been achieved. Many countries have gained independence, and colonialism is no longer the dominant global system it once was. However, there are still territories and people under colonial rule, and the legacy of colonialism continues to adversely impact the lives of millions of people worldwide. We reaffirm our commitment to the principles of the Declaration and the UN Charter, which emphasize the right to self-determination, sovereignty, and territorial integrity. We acknowledge the importance of addressing the ongoing challenges faced by colonial territories, including economic underdevelopment, social inequality, and environmental degradation. As we commemorate this anniversary, we call for renewed effort to support decolonization process, promote self-determination, and address the legacies of colonialism. We recognize the importance of international cooperation, dialogue, and solidarity in achieving these goals. Let us work together towards a future where all peoples can exercise their right to self-determination, live in dignity, and enjoy the benefits of independence and prosperity. Thank you, President.
I thank you, the distinguished representative of the United Republic of Tanzania. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Fiji.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Today, as we commemorate the 65th anniversary of the International Day against Colonialism, Knowledge Forms and Manifestations, We are reminded that decolonization process is not only a historical achievement, but a living symbol of the United Nations' enduring commitment to the principle of self-determination. It is in this principle that guarantees that non-self-governing territories have the right to decide their own political, economic, social, and cultural future. The rights of these territories are enshrined in Article 1, number 2, and Article 73 of the United Nations Charter, which must remain a moral compass guiding our collective work. On this basis, Fiji reaffirms its unwavering commitment to addressing the pending questions in support of the inalienable rights of the peoples of non-self-governing territories. As a member of the Special Committee on Decolonization of C-24, Fiji values the transparent process that enables dialogue between non-self-governing territories, administering powers, and the Member States. Yet we recognize that each situation is unique, requiring a tailored case-by-case approach. Some are politically sensitive and demand direct bilateral consultations. While such process may take longer, we must not lose momentum. climate change, natural disasters, access to finance, among others, is increasingly a need for these mostly small island states or small island territories. Fiji will remain active on this issue in C24 and in the Fourth Committee. Mr. President, the United Nations has achieved tremendous success in liberating more than 80 former colonies, who have since gained independence. It is imperative that our collective effort remains steadfast to dismantle the last remnants of colonialism in the 17 countries that remain, 17 territories. This requires meaningful dialogue, open and inclusive communication, and constructive collaboration to ensure peaceful transitions and to safeguard the rights of people, self-determination, free from external manipulation or coercion. In the Pacific region, where nearly a quarter of the remaining non-self-governing territories are situated, Fiji will remain guided by the 54th Pacific Islands Forum Communique and the 23rd Melanesian Spearhead Group Leaders Communique. We will continue to play our part in ensuring that sustained and inclusive political dialogue remains the pathways chosen by the people of these territories. To conclude, Fiji reiterates its commitment to defend the principles of the United Nations and to uphold the promise of the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples. On this 65th anniversary, let us renew our pledge to ensure that the unfinished mandate of decolonization is fulfilled and that all peoples may live in dignity, freedom, and self-determination. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Fiji. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Colombia.

President, allow me to begin by thanking you for convening this meeting, which invites us to consider the subject of decolonization, which is not a closed chapter in history. Rather, it is an unresolved task that requires consistency, constance, and political will. Colombia aligns itself with a statement by Uganda on behalf of the Non-Aligned Movement. And I would like to make the following comments in my national capacity. President, Sixty-five years have passed since the historic resolution 1514, which adopted the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples. Nevertheless, colonial situations and contemporary manifestations of domination persist. These run counter to the spirit of the United Nations Charter. President, Colombia rejects and unreservedly condemns all forms of colonialism, neocolonialism or imperialism. We oppose any narrative that normalizes structural inequalities and colonial hangovers in economic policies that perpetuate dependence. as well as policies that reproduce subordination, as well as threats or the use of force, non-consensual exploitation of resources in non-self-governing or disputed territories, unilateral coercive measures, which have affected millions of people around the world. Also, the perpetuation of inequalities through the international financial architecture, All of these are historic and contemporary manifestations of colonialism. Colombia unambiguously defends the right of all peoples to self-determination, the right to freely determine their political condition and to achieve their economic, social and cultural development. In that regard, Colombia reaffirms its commitment to the United Nations Charter, to resolution 1514 and supports the role of the Special Committee on Decolonization, the C-24. We hope that its work will once again demonstrate concrete progress. President, allow me to conclude by citing President Gustavo Petro. "Liberty, dignity and the rights of peoples cannot be taken away in America or in any part of the world. In Colombia, we are builders of life, of democracy, of liberty, and of humanity. In that spirit, Colombia raises its voice so that, for once and for all, the dream of justice, peace, and self-determination for all peoples can be a universal reality, a humanity that is free, and that allows for all of our differences to exist, which in actual fact represent our greatest source of wealth. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Colombia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Morocco.

Thank you, President. The Kingdom of Morocco has constructively committed, along with engaged with the co-sponsors during the negotiations and resolutions of the resolution 80/106 that convened this meeting. The Kingdom of Morocco voted in favour of that resolution, which called for the organization of this commemorative meeting. However, during this process, we were clear on the following points. our refusal to see this initiative be used against Member States, their territorial integrity and their national unity, in accordance with the spirit of the very declaration that we are commemorating today. the need for this initiative to be part of a thematic framework, bringing together Member States and not creating dangerous divisions among the members of this Assembly.
